an0049.user: Dental clinic. Narrow question — why is my CTR low? Last 30 days I had about 1.04M impressions, 14,064 clicks so CTR ~1.4%, but only 105 booked, which is a 0.75% conversion rate. AOV ₹1,250. Running broad-match keywords.
an0049.assistant:
Your CTR isn't your problem — 1.4% is fine. The number bleeding you is the 0.75% conversion, and it's a symptom of who you're paying to click, not how few click.

14,064 clicks producing 105 bookings means roughly 14,000 people clicked your ad and didn't book. That's not a copy or CTR failure; that's broad-match dragging in people searching loosely — 'tooth pain home remedy', 'is a root canal painful', 'dentist salary' — curiosity, not intent. They click because the ad's relevant to their search; they don't book because they were never shopping for a dentist.

So lifting CTR would just buy you more of the wrong clicks. The fix points the other way: kill broad-match, move to phrase and exact on genuine intent terms — 'dentist near me', 'root canal appointment [your city]', 'dental implant cost'. Build an aggressive negative-keyword list to block the informational junk. Your click volume will fall and your booking rate will climb, which is exactly the trade you want.

Stop optimising for clicks. For a clinic, the only metric that pays rent is cost per booked appointment — track that, not CTR.

an0050.user: Kids-coding edtech. I want the sophisticated read on an attribution mess. Post-iOS, the ad platform reports 3.4 ROAS but Shopify last-click says 1.4. ₹9.5L spend last month. I keep flip-flopping on which to believe and it's paralysing my budget decisions.
an0050.assistant:
The paralysis comes from a false premise — that one of them is correct. Neither is. They're two instruments calibrated to over- and under-count, and you're trying to average a liar and a pessimist.

The platform's 3.4 is inflated: post-iOS it models conversions it can no longer directly see and claims any sale within a 7-day click window, so it takes credit for enrolments it merely influenced. Shopify's last-click 1.4 is deflated: it gives the whole sale to the final touch — usually a parent Googling your brand after weeks of deliberation — and awards your top-of-funnel ad nothing for sparking interest. Truth is somewhere between 1.4 and 3.4, and the gap never closes because they disagree by design.

Stop adjudicating. Manage to blended CAC: ₹9.5L divided by the actual number of new paying students Shopify recorded last month. That's the real, all-in cost to acquire a customer, and no attribution window can spin it. Set it against what a student is worth — first course plus the likelihood they buy the next level — and your budget decision makes itself.

One edtech-specific note: your consideration cycle is long (parents deliberate for weeks), so last-click will undercount your ads worse than for impulse e-commerce. That's another reason to trust blended over either ROAS. Track it monthly; let the dashboards keep feuding.

an0052.assistant:
Start by leaving it alone. An 8% CAC move on 100 conversions in a single week is noise, not a degrading audience — that's well inside the normal week-to-week wobble of a sample that size. A handful of pricier conversions and CAC twitches 8% with nothing actually wrong underneath.

What would actually justify action: CAC rising in the same direction for 3–4 consecutive weeks, or a single jump big enough to clear the noise — think 25–30%+, not 8%. Keep the campaign exactly as is, log CAC each week, and reassess once you've got a month of data. There's no signal here to chase yet.
